newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Yachting: Peter Campbell's Rhumbline Column.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Yachting: Peter Campbell's Rhumbline Column.

text.p: By Peter Campbell*
OLYMPIC YACHTING WILL STAY IN SYDNEY

Despite much speculation and kite-flying, the yachting regatta of the Sydney 2000 Olympics will stay in Sydney, with some sailing on the Harbour, others just north and south of the Heads. There is no possible chance that the yachting might be moved to Melbourne or, in fact, to any venue beyond the immediate waters of Sydney.
As Australian Yachting Federation president BOB LUCAS stressed to me this week:
"These are Sydney's Games and it will be Sydney's regatta."

Adding weight were the comments of GLENN BOURKE, the champion sailor who this week took up duties with the Sydney Organising Committee for Olympic Games (SOCOG) as yachting competition manager for 2000, to the Sydney Morning Herald.

"We have the potential to stage the greatest yachting regatta ever," BOURKE was quoted as saying. "This is the most marvellous opportunity to showcase Sydney for the world, and put on the sort of racing that will appeal to competitors and spectators alike."

Nevertheless, just how many of the ten or eleven disciplines can be staged within the Harbour may hinge on a special Sydney 2000 Trial Regatta on October 1, 2 and 3. Three officials of the International Sailing Federation (ISAF) and a leading member of the International Olympic Committee are coming to Sydney that week to look closely at the Harbour, where and how the courses will fit, and the standard of race management.
The ISAF want to make Sydney a showcase of sailing, to not only provide the best and fairest courses for the athletes but to make it a spectacular sport for the public and the media.

Only keen sailing enthusiasts probably even know that sailing is an Olympic sport, in spite of the outstanding performance by our Aussie sailors at Savannah where they won a silver and a bronze medal, with eight competitors finishing in the top ten.

Television coverage here was limited to a total of some 15 minutes and only a couple of daily newspapers provided extensive coverage. In the U.S., the only television of the yachting was on the local station at Savannah.

Sydney Harbour offers the greatest opportunity ever to promote sailing to the public, nationally and internationally. Sydney Harbour is the perfect amphitheatre, an outstanding sailing venue for classes such as the new skiff-style dinghy to be introduced in 2000, as well as for the existing double-handed and single-handed dinghies and the sailboards.
We have a proven Olympic circle area seaward of Manly which would be ideal for the bigger keelboats and the multihull class, while a similar course could be set offshore, just south of the Heads.

What needs to be determined as soon as possible is the exact site of the shorebase for the yachts and the regatta administration. Apart from launching and mooring facilities, the yachting venue requires an extensive rigging area, storage area for the teams and large facilities for boat and sail measuring, race control, media and so on.
All this is not just for 2000 -- at least two pre-Olympic regattas must be held in Sydney in 1998 and 1999.

Originally, the foreshores of Rushcutters Bay adjacent to the Cruising Yacht Club of Australia were proposed as the Olympic yachting site but there appears to be strong resident opposition and council apathy.

The Yachting Association of New South Wales (NSWYA) is pushing strongly for Chowder Bay, Mosman, where current military facilities are expected to become vacant before 2000. The NSWYA sees this area, which has an extensive parkland behind a good beach and an existing wharf, as a legacy for sailing by subsequently becoming a National Sailing Centre for Australia.

The early October regatta will include some Olympic classes, among them the Laser dinghy, but in addition many of the nation's best youth sailors will be competing in what could be a vital regatta to ensure we have as many classes as possible sailing within the Harbour in 2000.

Meanwhile, the ISAF this week begins evaluation trials on Lake Garda, Italy, as a lead-up to the selection of the new high performance skiff-type dinghy for 2000. Among the classes being considered are two Australian boats, the B-14 and the 49er, designed by FRANK BETHWAITE and his son, JULIAN.

The classes for 2000 will be chosen by the ISAF at its annual meeting in November, while the report on the Olympic courses in Sydney will also be tabled at this international gathering of the world's leading yachting administrators.
I understand SOCOG has been given until early next year to decide the shore base venue.
SUMMER SAILING SEASON OPENS TOMORROW

Sydney's summer sailing season officially opens on Saturday with the Royal Sydney Yacht Squadron and Middle Harbour Yacht Club (MHYC) maintaining the tradition of sail pasts and the Cruising Yacht Club of Australia (CYCA) running the first short offshore race off the Heads.

The Squadron's parade of sail will start at 1100 hours with Rear Admiral DAVID CAMPBELL, AM RAN, taking the salute from the Kirribilli clubhouse. At MHYC, SIR JAMES HARDY will take the salute as a big fleet sails up Middle Harbour.
The CYCA has received more than 30 entries for its opening race, despite the fact that many ocean racing yachts are still on their way back from the big regattas in Queensland.

Club officials are forecasting a significant increase in competitors this year, both in keelboats and dinghy classes, with yachting on a high note following the excellent performance of our team Savannah and the win by SYD FISCHER and his team at the Kenwood Cup in Hawaii.
DEJA VU IN THE 18-FOOTERS

SORENSEN, RAMSDEN, BARNABAS, WINNING -- you would be excused for thinking you were reading a sailing report from the 1970s, but actually they will be part of the line-up for the Australian 18-Footers League season which gets underway on Sydney Harbour on Sunday week, September 18, with the ALF BEASHEL Memorial Trophy Race.
Many of the legends of 18-footer racing have been lured back to the League this season and are set to give a new generation of skiff sailors a run for their money.

Meanwhile, Grand Prix Sailing will have an added star this season in America's Cup winning skipper and world match racing champion RUSSELL COUTTS. The New Zealander will slot into the Grand Prix circuit in between his match-racing and other international commitments.
The Grand Prix 18-footer competition this summer will take in venues around Australia and New Zealand from October through to February.
COUTTS BEATS GILMOUR IN BRUT CUP
RUSSELL COUTTS dominates the world match racing scene, taking first place this week in the Brut Cup of New York from Australia's PETER GILMOUR.

COUTTS won the Brut Sailing Series earlier this year while GILMOUR'S successes this year have included winning the Swedish Match Race Cup, the ACI Ronhill Cup and the Eunos Australia Cup. He is still third in the world rankings, headed by COUTTS and American ED BAIRD, but now only seven points behind BAIRD.
AUSTRALIAN WOMEN FOR MATCH RACING

Sydney women sailors SUSAN WALTERS, KARYN GOJNICH and ALEX MURRAY flew out this week to compete in the 1996 Women's International Match Race Championship at Marblehead in the U.S. With the International Sailing Federation proposing an 11th gold medal, for women's match racing, at the 2000 Olympic regatta, the event has attracted competitors from Bermuda, Denmark, Germany, Canada and the U.S. as well as Australia.

The women will sail identical Sonar class keelboats with the Australians expecting tough competition from American BETSY ALISON, the current Rolex International Women's champion, and MARIE BOSERUP KLOK from Denmark, currently ranked number two in the Omega women's world match racing ranking list.
The Australian team, led by WALTERS, a Sydney mother of two, won the prestigious IYRU Nations Cup match racing series in San Francisco last September, beating the U.S. in the final 3-0.
Olympian GOJNICH will be again calling tactics, with MURRAY on the bow and WALTERS helming.
"We are very excited about the prospect of competing in Sydney 2000," WALTERS said before flying to the U.S. "This regatta is the start of our preparation."
*Peter Campbell is editor of Offshore Yachting magazine.
